explainers.title: Hello again, and welcome to Evaluation
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. You have already grown two of the six thinking skills this year. In Research you learned to find out about an issue in a careful, organised way. In Analysis you learned to break an issue into parts and ask why things happen. Now you are ready for the third skill: Evaluation.

Here are all six thinking skills again, so you can see where this unit fits:

In Research you gathered lots of sources of information. But here is the thing: not every source is worth using. Some are helpful, some are out of date, and some are only trying to sell you something. Evaluation is the skill of weighing each source so you know which ones to trust. Think of it like choosing fruit at the market: you do not put every mango in your basket. You pick them up, look them over, and keep the good ones. Evaluation teaches you to do the very same thing with information.

Why does this matter beyond school? Every day, grown-ups are told all sorts of things by adverts, by the internet, by people with something to gain. A parent reading two claims about a medicine, a shopper deciding whether a bargain is real, a voter listening to two leaders: all of them need to judge who to trust. A learner who practises evaluation now will be much harder to fool, for their whole life. That is why this skill is so powerful.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how useful, trustworthy or strong something really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way, which means three kinds of support work together:

In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss as a class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. Evaluation especially loves a good discussion, because talking through a source out loud helps you spot its strengths and weaknesses. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it as a real conversation.

Your evaluation skill will grow in three stages this year, just as it did for Research. You will begin by starting each skill, then move on to developing it, and finally you will get better at it. Do not worry if judging a source feels tricky at first. Even grown-ups get it wrong sometimes. Starting is meant to feel like a first try.
bullets: You, at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a friendly study partner and a whole class rolled into one. It will discuss your ideas, disagree with you kindly, and give you feedback at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best work, ask the questions that matter most, and hear how other learners judged the same sources.

explainers.title: Meet Talia, our evaluator for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 6 learner all the way through the unit. Her name is Talia, and she is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

Talia cares about healthy eating. Her class has been growing tomatoes and herbs in the school garden, and they want to help everyone at Ehel Academy eat food that is both healthy and kind to the planet. Then, one morning, a big bright advert appears on a wall right by the school gate. It shows a fizzy sugary drink called Mango Fizz, and it makes the drink look cool, fun and refreshing. Talia stops and stares at it. She wonders: is this advert telling the whole truth, and should it really be right next to a school that is trying to teach healthy eating?

That question opens Talia's whole project for this unit. To answer it well, she cannot just trust her feelings. She has to gather sources about healthy eating and about the advert, and then work out which ones are useful, who made them, why they made them, and what she truly thinks. In other words, she has to evaluate. As you meet each new skill, you will see exactly what Talia does with it, and you will do the same with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is an issue that matters both in the wider world and right where you live. In this unit you will collect a small set of sources about your issue, evaluate each one, and use the best of them to suggest a fair action, just as Talia will.

Here are four issues that are big all around the world and also very real in the Horn of Africa. Any of these could become your Challenge:

Your classmates will care about different things. Talia is drawn to healthy eating and the advert. Idris worries that younger children are not safe online. Leila is upset by the plastic bottles left around the schoolyard, and by the ones that wash up along the coast near Berbera. The same problems fill streets in towns right across the Horn of Africa, from Hargeisa to Mogadishu. Any of these could grow into a strong Challenge.

You do not have to choose right now. As you work through the skills, keep a note of any issue that makes you curious, or that gives you a little 'that is not fair' feeling. Strong curiosity and that sense of unfairness are excellent signs of a good Challenge topic.
bullets: Healthy and sustainable eating — helping people choose food that is good for them and gentle on the planet.
Adverts near school — such as the Mango Fizz advert, and whether adverts for sugary food and drinks belong next to a school.
Staying safe online — helping younger children use the internet safely (the digital world).
Single-use plastic — cutting down waste, and perhaps setting up a recycling point at school.

explainers.title: So what is evaluation?
explainers.body:
In everyday life, to evaluate something means to decide how good or how useful it is. In Global Perspectives, evaluation means deciding how useful a source is for a particular purpose, and how far you can trust it. You do this by asking two simple questions about every source: who made it, and why did they make it?

Evaluation has three main parts, and this unit teaches all three:

Notice that evaluation is not about calling a source 'good' or 'bad'. It is more careful than that. A source can be brilliant for one job and useless for another. A recipe is a wonderful source if you want to cook, but a poor source if you want to know what people think about healthy eating. Evaluation is all about matching a source to your purpose.
bullets: Judging how useful a source is, by thinking about who made it and what its purpose was.
Weighing a source's strengths (what it is good at) and its limitations (what it cannot tell you).
Giving your own opinion about other people's perspectives, saying clearly where you agree and where you disagree.

explainers.title: Skill 1: The purpose of a source - why was it made?
explainers.body:
Every source is made for a purpose. The purpose is the reason someone made it: what they were trying to do. Once you know a source's purpose, you understand it much better, because purpose changes how useful a source is and what it is good at.

Here are some common purposes a source can have:
bullets: To explain how or why something happens, such as a textbook page.
To change your mind or persuade you, such as a campaign poster.
To tell you how to do or make something, such as a recipe.
To give both sides of an argument fairly, such as a balanced article.
To describe what something is, such as an encyclopedia entry.

explainers.title: Skill 2: The strengths and limitations of a source
explainers.body:
No source is perfect. Every source has strengths, the things it is good at, and limitations, the things it is not good at or cannot tell you. A skilled evaluator names both, instead of just saying 'I like it' or 'I do not like it'.

The trick is to think about what a source can and cannot give you. A source might be clear, or written by an expert, or full of real examples: those are strengths. But the same source might be out of date, or only show one side, or not really be about your issue: those are limitations.

explainers.title: Skill 3: How useful is a source for my goal?
explainers.body:
Now put purpose, strengths and limitations together to decide the big question: how useful is this source for what I am trying to do? A source is not useful or useless on its own. It is useful, or not, for a particular goal. So always ask: useful for what?

A simple way to do this is to fill in two sentences for each source: it is useful because ..., and it is not so useful for .... When you can finish both, you have really evaluated the source.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Who made it? Thinking about the author
explainers.body:
The very first evaluation question is 'who?'. The person or group who made a source is called the author or creator. Knowing who made a source, and whether they really know about the topic, tells you a great deal about how far to trust it.

When you meet a new source, ask yourself three quick things about its author:
bullets: Who made it — a named person, a group, a company, or nobody you can see?
What do they know — is it their job, or their subject, or are they just guessing?
Why did they make it — to help you understand, or to get something from you?

explainers.title: Skill 5: The perspective of a source
explainers.body:
Everyone sees the world from their own point of view, and so does every source. This point of view is called a perspective. A source's perspective is shaped by who made it and what they want. Spotting the perspective of a source is a key part of evaluation, because it explains why a source says what it says.

A source is not bad just because it has a perspective. Almost every source has one. The skill is to notice it, so you are not swept along without realising.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Facts and opinions - and why you need both
explainers.body:
Sources are full of two different things, and a good evaluator can tell them apart. A factual claim is something that can be checked against reliable evidence. An opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with. Perspectives are shaped by opinions, values, experiences and evidence.

Some sources give mainly facts, and some give mainly opinions or perspectives. Being able to sort them helps you know what each source is for.
bullets: Fact: a can of Mango Fizz contains about nine spoons of sugar. You could check this on the label.
Opinion: adverts for sugary drinks should not be allowed near a primary school. Someone could reasonably disagree.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Choosing, comparing and scoring your sources
explainers.body:
When you have several sources, you have to choose the best ones and be able to give a reason for your choice. A strong way to do this is to compare what different sources say, and even to score them for usefulness, giving each a number.

Scoring sounds hard, but it is simple. Put your sources in order from most useful to least useful for your goal, and write one reason for each place. The reason matters as much as the number, because it shows you really thought about it.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Using sources to justify an action
explainers.body:
In Global Perspectives, evaluation leads somewhere: to a fair action you can suggest. To justify an action means to give good reasons for it, and your best reasons come from the sources you have judged to be strong. A source that supports your action makes your case much more convincing.

When you are ready to suggest an action, you can lay it out in four clear parts:
bullets: My issue — the problem I care about.
My action — the fair, doable change I am suggesting.
My sources — the strongest sources I found.
How they support my action — the reason each source backs my idea.

explainers.title: Skill 9: Can I trust it? Expertise, relevance and bias
explainers.body: This is the heart of evaluation: deciding how far to trust a source. Three tests help you decide. Ask about expertise (does the maker really know the topic?), relevance (is it actually about my issue?), and bias (does it lean unfairly to one side?).
bullets: Expertise: a source made by an expert, such as a scientist on their subject, is usually more trustworthy.
Relevance: a source is only useful if it is really about your issue, not just near it.
Bias: a biased source leans one way on purpose, often because the maker has something to gain.

explainers.title: Skill 10: Agreeing and disagreeing with a perspective
explainers.body:
Evaluation is not only about sources. It is also about saying what you think of other people's perspectives. When you hear someone's view, you can agree, disagree, or land somewhere in between. The clever part is that agreeing is not all-or-nothing. You can sit anywhere on a spectrum, from strongly agree to strongly disagree.

Here is the spectrum you will use. When you hear a perspective, decide where you sit, and always give your reason:
bullets: Strongly agree — I think this is completely right.
Agree — I mostly think this is right.
Not sure — I can see both sides, or I need more information.
Disagree — I mostly think this is not right.
Strongly disagree — I think this is completely wrong.

explainers.title: Skill 11: Writing your own evaluation of a source
explainers.body: Now you bring every skill together to write your own evaluation of a single source. A written evaluation is a short piece where you weigh a source fairly and say what you think of it. Use this frame, which follows the skills you have learned:
bullets: Who wrote it? Name the author or creator, and what they know.
What is it for? Say the purpose and the perspective.
Identify a point. Pick one clear thing the source says.
Comment on it. Use your own knowledge to give its strengths and limitations.
Give your view. Say whether you agree or disagree with the point, and why.

explainers.title: How evaluation feeds the other five skills
explainers.body:
Evaluation is the third Global Perspectives skill, and it sits right in the middle for a reason: it connects to all the others.

So the care you take in evaluation now is never wasted. It makes every other skill sharper, and it protects you from being fooled by sources that only look good on the surface.
bullets: Research gives you the sources; evaluation decides which ones are worth using.
Analysis breaks a source's argument into parts; evaluation judges how strong that argument really is.
Reflection grows every time you notice how a source, or your tutor, changed your mind.
Collaboration works better when you can weigh other people's sources and perspectives fairly, without falling out.
Communication is far stronger when you back your message with sources you have judged to be trustworthy.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the evaluation cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every evaluation skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into one smooth cycle you can use for any source:
bullets: Ask who made it, and why (the author and the purpose).
Name its perspective, and sort its facts from its opinions.
Weigh its strengths and its limitations.
Test it for expertise, relevance and bias to decide how far to trust it.
Decide how useful it is for your particular goal.
Say what you think, agreeing or disagreeing on the spectrum, with a reason.
Use your strongest sources to justify a fair action.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Reflection. Once you can evaluate sources and perspectives, reflection teaches you to turn that same careful, fair thinking on yourself: how you learn, how you changed your mind, and what you will do better next time. Strong evaluation now will make strong reflection much easier later. Well done for growing a skill that will keep you wise for the rest of your life.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
We will use real topics such as healthy food, adverts, staying safe online and plastic waste.
But the real prize is not to become an expert on food or plastic. It is to become someone who can look at any source and decide, calmly, how far to trust it.

bigIdeas.title: The four big questions an evaluator asks
lines: Who is the author or creator of this source?
What was their purpose, and what is their perspective?
What are the strengths and limitations of the source?
How useful and trustworthy is it for my goal, and what do I think?

bigIdeas.title: Strengths and limitations, side by side
lines: A science page on how the body uses sugar. Strength: clear, checked facts. Limitation: it will not tell you what to do about the advert.
A leaflet from a healthy-eating group. Strength: strong reasons to eat well. Limitation: it shows only one side.
A newspaper story about a local school garden. Strength: a real, nearby example. Limitation: one garden may not be true for everywhere.

bigIdeas.title: Perspective is not the same as being wrong
lines: A source with a strong perspective can still contain true facts.
A source that tries to be balanced can still miss something important.
Your job is not to throw away every source with a perspective. It is to notice the perspective and weigh the source with your eyes open.

bigIdeas.title: A source is not wrong just because it has a bias
lines: A biased source can still contain useful facts.
But when a maker has something to gain, such as a company selling a drink, check its claims against a fairer source.
Being fair does not mean trusting nobody. It means noticing who gains, and weighing the source with care.

bigIdeas.title: A finished model evaluation
lines: This leaflet was made by a healthy-eating group whose job is to help people eat well.
Its purpose is to persuade, and its perspective is that we should all eat less sugar.
One point it makes is that sugary drinks harm children's teeth.
A strength is that it gives clear reasons; a limitation is that it shows only one side.
I agree, because the science on sugar and teeth is strong, but I would still check a second source.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one issue that matters both in the world and where you live. This is your Challenge.
Good choices for this unit: healthy eating, adverts near school, staying safe online, or single-use plastic.
You will gather and judge sources about it, and by the end you will have written your own evaluation.

bigIdeas.title: The advert, described in words
lines: A bright poster shows a cold, fizzing bottle of Mango Fizz with happy children playing football.
The big words say: Mango Fizz — the fun, refreshing taste of real mango!
In tiny letters at the bottom it says: contains added sugar.
The poster is on a wall right beside the Ehel Academy gate.

bigIdeas.title: Remember the four classmates
lines: Talia agreed the adverts should be limited, because children are easily influenced.
Karim agreed children are influenced, but felt persuading is better than banning.
Nadia strongly agreed, because young children cannot always tell an advert is selling something.
Omar disagreed, because he felt his little brother does not even notice adverts.

models.title: Evaluation happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine your friend says a certain shop sells the best sambusas in town.
You do not just believe it at once. You ask yourself: does my friend really know? Have they tried many shops, or just this one?
Then a poster outside the shop says exactly the same thing. You trust the poster less, because the shop made it to sell you sambusas.
Weighing your friend and the poster, and deciding who to trust, is real evaluation. You already do it.

So evaluation is not a strange, school-only activity. It is a calm, fair way of weighing what you are told, and you can get better and better at it. In this unit you will simply learn to do it on purpose, with more skill, and about sources that matter to your community.

models.title: Talia matches her food sources to their purpose
lines: A recipe card for a mango smoothie: its purpose is to tell you how to make something.
A poster from a healthy-eating campaign: its purpose is to change people's minds.
An encyclopedia entry on 'a balanced diet': its purpose is to describe what something is.
A balanced article, Is it better to eat less meat? For and against: its purpose is to give both sides.
A Mango Fizz advert: its purpose is to make you want to buy the drink.

See how knowing the purpose already tells Talia a lot? The advert's purpose is to sell, so she will be careful before trusting its claims. The balanced article's purpose is to give both sides, so it may be fairer. Purpose is the first clue in every evaluation.

models.title: Talia weighs a smoothie recipe
lines: Talia finds a recipe for a fruit smoothie made from local mangoes and bananas.
A strength: her class could actually make it and taste it, which proves that healthy food can taste wonderful.
A limitation: the recipe will not tell her what different people think about healthy eating, or why some families find it hard.
So the recipe is useful for one job and not for another. Naming both is the skill.

models.title: Talia builds a useful-because table
lines: Talia's goal: to help her school choose food that is healthy and sustainable.
The smoothie recipe is useful because the class can make and taste it; it is not so useful for hearing different people's views.
The encyclopedia entry is useful because it gives clear, checked facts; it is not so useful for suggesting an action.
The healthy-eating leaflet is useful because it gives strong reasons to act; it is not so useful for showing both sides.

One more question makes evaluation really practical. Ask: which of my sources best suggests an action? In Global Perspectives you gather information not just to know more, but to help make something better. The source that points to a fair, doable action is often the most useful of all.

models.title: Idris checks who wrote two online-safety leaflets
lines: Idris is looking at staying safe online. He finds two leaflets.
One is made by a well-known internet-safety group, written by named people whose job is online safety, and updated this year.
The other has no author's name, no date, and it keeps pushing you to click a link.
Idris trusts the first far more, because he can see who made it and that they really know the topic.

A source with no author is not always wrong, but it should make you careful. If you cannot tell who made something, or why, you cannot be sure it is fair. Always try to find the author before you rely on a source.

models.title: Talia names the perspective of three sources
lines: A Mango Fizz advert. Perspective: our drink is fun and refreshing, and you should buy it.
A leaflet from a group that wants people to eat less meat. Perspective: eating less meat is better for you and the planet.
A balanced for-and-against article on vegetarian meals. Perspective: there are good points on both sides, so decide for yourself.
Talia can now see that the advert and the leaflet each push one way, while the balanced article tries to stay in the middle.

models.title: Talia sorts sources by facts or perspectives
lines: An encyclopedia entry on sugar: mainly facts.
A campaign leaflet, Five reasons to cut sugary drinks now: mainly opinions and perspectives.
A report comparing school-meal rules in different countries: mainly facts.
A newspaper column, Why these adverts must go: mainly opinions and perspectives.

Here is the clever part, and it surprises many learners. To persuade people, you usually need both facts and opinions together. A fact on its own does not tell people what to do. An opinion on its own is not seen as a good reason. But join them, and they become powerful: 'A can of Mango Fizz has about nine spoons of sugar (fact), so I think these adverts should not be by our school gate (opinion).' The fact gives the opinion its strength.

models.title: Leila scores four sources about plastic waste
lines: Leila wants to persuade the school to set up a recycling point. She scores four sources from 1, most useful, to 4, least useful.
1: a scientific report on how plastic harms sea animals, because it is expert and closely about her issue.
2: a blog by local residents about litter in the park, because it shows nearby people want the mess cleaned up.
3: a brochure from a recycling company, because it gives useful facts but only shows its own side.
4: an advert for water sold in plastic bottles, because it is only publicity and goes against her message.

Once she has scored them, Leila can pick the most useful source to lead with, and keep the others to back it up. Comparing and scoring turns a messy pile of sources into a clear order you can explain to anyone.

models.title: Talia justifies her action with sources
lines: Talia's issue: sugary-drink adverts sit right beside a school teaching healthy eating.
Her action: ask the school to add a water-refill point and a healthy-eating display by the gate.
Her sources: a science page on sugar, a report on school-meal rules, and her own class survey.
How they support it: the science page shows sugar is harmful, the report shows other schools act, and the survey shows her classmates would use a refill point.

Notice that Talia does not just say 'I feel strongly about this'. She points to sources. Backing an action with evaluated sources is what turns a feeling into a fair, convincing case that adults will listen to.

models.title: Leila's group tests six sources for a recycling point
lines: A scientific report on plastic harming ocean wildlife: really useful, because of its expert perspective.
A radio interview with a politician about raising money: not really about the issue, so it is off-topic.
A blog by local residents about park litter: pretty useful, because local people want the mess stopped.
An advert for water in plastic bottles: not useful at all, because it is a drinks company's publicity and biased.
A newspaper story about shops charging for plastic bags: useful and closely relevant.
A brochure from a recycling company: some use, but one-sided, because the company wants to sell its service.

models.title: Four classmates give their perspective on the advert
lines: The question: should sugary-drink adverts near school be banned?
Talia: I agree they should be limited, because young children see them and are easily influenced.
Karim: I agree children are influenced, but banning is not the answer; we should persuade people instead.
Nadia: I strongly agree, because young children cannot always tell an advert is trying to sell them something.
Omar: I disagree, because my little brother never even notices adverts, so I think they do little harm.

Notice that these four do not simply say yes or no. Each one lands at a different place on the spectrum, and each gives a reason. That is exactly what a strong evaluator does: they respond to a perspective thoughtfully, and they can explain why they agree a little, a lot, or not at all.

models.title: Talia writes a short evaluation of the Mango Fizz advert
lines: Who wrote it: a drinks company, whose job is to sell drinks.
What it is for: to make the drink look fun and to get people to buy it; its perspective is that Mango Fizz is a great choice.
A point: the advert says the drink is refreshing and full of real mango.
Comment: a strength is that it is bright and clear; a limitation is that it never mentions the sugar or shows the other side.
Talia's view: I disagree that this is a great choice near a school, because the advert hides how much sugar the drink contains.

That is a complete evaluation. Talia named who made it and why, chose one point, weighed it with her own knowledge, and gave her honest view with a reason. When you can do this for a source of your own, you have truly learned to evaluate. You will practise writing one in the Activities file.

models.title: Talia's whole journey, from advert to action
lines: Skills 1 to 3: she found the purpose, strengths and usefulness of each food source.
Skills 4 and 5: she checked who made each source and named its perspective.
Skill 6: she sorted facts from opinions, and joined them to persuade.
Skills 7 and 9: she scored her sources and tested them for expertise, relevance and bias.
Skills 10 and 11: she said what she thought on the spectrum and wrote her own evaluation.
Skill 8: she used her strongest sources to justify asking for a water-refill point and a healthy-eating display.

By following this cycle, Talia turned a single advert on a wall into a fair, well-supported case she can share with her teacher and her school. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle on your own Challenge, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model: fact or opinion?
lines: A can of Mango Fizz has about nine spoons of sugar: this is a fact, because you could check it on the label.
Mango Fizz is the best drink in the world: this is an opinion, because it is what someone thinks and others could disagree.
Both sentences are about the same drink. The difference is only whether they can be checked.

Then try the clever step from the Lesson: choose one fact and one opinion from your own issue, and join them into a single persuasive sentence, such as: 'A can of Mango Fizz has about nine spoons of sugar, so I think these adverts should not be by our school.'

models.title: A model: being a source detective
lines: Source: a leaflet from a group that wants people to eat less meat.
Who made it: a named campaign group whose subject is food and the planet.
Why they made it: to persuade people to change what they eat.
Its perspective: eating less meat is better for you and better for the Earth.

models.title: A model: weighing a school-garden news story
lines: Source: a newspaper story about a school that grew its own vegetables.
Strengths: it is a real, nearby example, and it shows an action that actually worked.
Limitations: it is about one school only, so it may not be true everywhere.
Overall: useful for showing that an action is possible, but not for proving it would work at every school.

models.title: A model: scoring sources about staying safe online
lines: Goal: help younger children stay safe online.
1: a leaflet from a named internet-safety group, because it is expert and closely about the issue.
2: a news story about a real scam, because it shows why the issue matters.
3: a survey of which games children play, because it is only a little bit about safety.

models.title: A model: justifying an action about plastic
lines: Issue: too many plastic bottles are left around the schoolyard.
Action: I think we could set up a recycling point by the school gate.
Source 1, a scientific report: it shows plastic harms sea animals, so cutting waste matters.
Source 2, a residents' blog: it shows local people already want the litter cleaned up.

models.title: A model evaluation, to guide you
lines: This leaflet was written by a healthy-eating group whose job is to help people eat well.
Its purpose is to persuade, and its perspective is that we should all eat less sugar.
One point it makes is that sugary drinks harm children's teeth.
A strength is that it gives clear reasons; a limitation is that it shows only one side.
I agree with the point, because the science on sugar and teeth is strong, but I would check a second source too.

toolkit.title: The evaluation cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your source, good evaluation follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Who and why: find the author and the purpose.
Perspective: name the source's point of view.
Facts or opinions: sort what it says.
Strengths and limitations: weigh what it is good at and not good at.
Trust: test it for expertise, relevance and bias.
Usefulness: decide how useful it is for your goal.
Your view: agree or disagree on the spectrum, with a reason.
Justify: use your strongest sources to support a fair action.

toolkit.title: The Evaluation skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Evaluation means deciding how useful a source is for a particular purpose, and how far you can trust it. You do this by asking who made a source and why, weighing its strengths and limitations, and giving your own opinion about the perspectives you meet.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, never judge a source as simply 'good' or 'bad'; ask 'useful for what?'. Second, be fair: notice a source's perspective and weigh it with your eyes open, instead of believing it or throwing it away at once. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

You will use this skill far beyond Global Perspectives. Every time an advert, a website or even a friend tells you something, you can pause and quietly ask: who is telling me this, and why? That one small habit, practised often, will keep you thinking clearly for the rest of your life.

toolkit.title: A one-minute check for any source
toolkit.intro: When you do not have much time, run this fast version of the cycle. It catches most problems in under a minute, and you can do the full cycle later for your most important sources.
items: Who made it, and do they really know the topic?
Why did they make it: to help me, or to gain something?
Fact or opinion: is it something I could check, or just what they think?
Relevant: is it truly about my issue, or only near it?
So what: how far will I trust it, and how will I use it?

toolkit.title: Your Stage 6 Evaluation learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your evaluation skill grows in three stages this year. Here are the real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: A guide to the purpose of a source
toolkit.intro: Every source is made for a reason. Work out the purpose first, because it changes how useful a source is and how far to trust it. If the purpose is hard to spot, look at who made the source and what they might gain, because the purpose is usually hiding there.

rows: To explain
It shows how or why something happens.
A textbook page on how the body uses sugar.
To describe
It outlines what something is.
An encyclopedia entry on a balanced diet.
To instruct
It tells you how to do or make something.
A recipe card for a fruit smoothie.
To persuade
It tries to change your mind.
A healthy-eating campaign poster.
To sell
It wants you to buy something.
A Mango Fizz advert.
To balance
It gives both sides fairly.
A for-and-against article on eating less meat.

toolkit.title: Strengths - what is it good at?
items: Is it clear and easy to understand?
Was it made by someone who knows the topic?
Does it give real examples or checked facts?
Is it closely about my issue?

toolkit.title: Limitations - what is it not good at?
toolkit.intro: When you can name at least one strength and one limitation, you have truly weighed a source, instead of just reacting to it. If you can find only strengths, or only limitations, look again, because almost every source has some of each.
items: Is it out of date?
Does it show only one side?
Does the maker have something to gain?
Is it really about my issue, or only near it?

toolkit.title: Who wrote it, why, and can I trust it?
toolkit.intro:
This is the core of evaluation. Ask 'who?' and 'why?', then run the three trust tests.

Remember: a source is not wrong just because it has a perspective or a bias. Notice who gains, then check its claims against a fairer source.

A quick way to test for bias is to ask one question: would this maker lose anything by telling the whole truth? If the answer is yes, such as a company that wants to sell you a drink, read the source with extra care.

rows: Who made it?
Find the author or creator.
A named person, a group, a company, or nobody shown?
Why did they make it?
Find the purpose.
To help you understand, or to get something from you?
Expertise
Do they really know the topic?
An expert on the subject is usually more trustworthy.
Relevance
Is it really about my issue?
A source can be interesting but off-topic.
Bias
Does it lean unfairly to one side?
A maker who gains, such as a seller, may be biased.

toolkit.title: Facts and perspectives: a quick sorter
toolkit.intro:
Sort what a source says, then remember that to persuade you usually need both.

To persuade well, join a fact and an opinion: 'This drink has about nine spoons of sugar (fact), so I think the advert should not be by our school (opinion).'

Opinion words such as best, worst, should, terrible or amazing are clues that you are reading an opinion, not a fact. When you spot one, slow down and ask whether the source can back it up.

rows: Fact
Can be checked and shown to be true.
A can of this drink has about nine spoons of sugar.
Opinion
What someone thinks; others may disagree.
This drink should not be advertised near school.
Perspective
A whole point of view, built from opinions.
Our group thinks all sugary adverts should go.

toolkit.title: The agree and disagree spectrum
toolkit.intro:
When you hear someone's perspective, decide where you sit, and always give a reason. You do not have to be all-or-nothing.

Sentence starters: 'I agree with ... because ...', 'I disagree with ... because ...', 'I can see why ... thinks that, but I ...'.

It is fine to sit in the middle at 'not sure', especially when you still need more information. A thoughtful 'not sure', with a reason, is far stronger than a quick yes or no with nothing behind it.

rows: Strongly agree
I think this is completely right.
Agree
I mostly think this is right.
Not sure
I can see both sides, or I need more information.
Disagree
I mostly think this is not right.
Strongly disagree
I think this is completely wrong.

toolkit.title: Frame: write your own evaluation
toolkit.intro:
Use this five-step frame to write a short, fair evaluation of any source. Aim for one short paragraph.

Sentence starters you can use: 'This source was made by ...', 'Its purpose is to ...', 'One point it makes is ...', 'A strength is ..., but a limitation is ...', 'I agree / disagree with this because ...'.
items: Who wrote it? Name the author and what they know.
What is it for? Give the purpose and the perspective.
Identify a point. Pick one clear thing the source says.
Comment on it. Use your knowledge to give its strengths and limitations.
Give your view. Say whether you agree or disagree with the point, and why.

checklists.title: Checklist: strengths and limitations
checklists.intro: A strong evaluation always names both. Ask these questions about every source.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'evaluation' mean?
practice.answer: Evaluation means deciding how useful a source is for a purpose, and how far you can trust it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: The two big questions you ask about every source are 'who?' and '______?'.
practice.answer: Why? (You ask 'who made it?' and 'why did they make it?'.)

practice.prompt: The reason a source was made is called its ______.
practice.answer: Its purpose.

practice.prompt: The things a source is good at are its strengths. The things it is not good at are its ______.
practice.answer: Its limitations.

practice.prompt: True or false: a source is either useful or useless, no matter what your goal is.
practice.answer: False. A source is useful, or not, for a particular goal; it can be great for one job and poor for another.

practice.answer: The author (or creator).

practice.prompt: The point of view a source has is called its ______.
practice.answer: Its perspective.

practice.answer: Opinions (facts and opinions together are the most persuasive).

practice.prompt: Name the three tests you use to decide how far to trust a source.
practice.answer: Expertise, relevance and bias.

practice.answer: Bias.

practice.answer: Reasons.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why a source with no author should make you careful.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Idris finds a leaflet about online safety with no author's name and no date. Should he trust it fully? Explain, using the word author.
practice.answer: No. With no author, Idris cannot tell who made it or whether they know about online safety, so he cannot be sure it is fair. He should find a source with a named, expert author.

practice.prompt: Leila has an advert from a company that sells plastic bottles, and a scientific report on plastic pollution. Which should she trust more for her recycling project, and why?
practice.answer: The scientific report, because it comes from experts on the topic, while the advert is biased, as the company wants to sell plastic bottles.

practice.prompt: Talia reads that Mango Fizz is 'the best drink in the world'. Is that a fact or an opinion, and how do you know?
practice.answer: An opinion, because 'the best in the world' is what someone thinks, and others could disagree; it cannot be checked and proved.

practice.prompt: Nadia wants to persuade her school to serve fruit at break. She has one fact about sugar and one strong opinion. Why is it better to use both together?
practice.answer: The fact gives a solid reason, and the opinion says what to do about it. A fact alone does not tell people to act, and an opinion alone is not seen as a good reason, so together they persuade best.

practice.prompt: Omar says an advert is a great source about healthy eating. What is the problem with using an advert this way? Use the word bias.
practice.answer: An advert is biased, because its purpose is to sell, so it only shows the good side and hides anything unhelpful. It is not a fair source about healthy eating.

vocabulary.meaning: The sensible steps you suggest to help make an issue better.
The reasons someone gives to try to convince you of something.
Things that can be checked and shown to be true.
What you learn or discover after looking into something.
When something changes what you think, feel or do.
To give good reasons for a choice or an action.
The things a source is not good at, or cannot tell you.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
The points of view people have, shaped by who they are.
The reason a source was made; what it is for.
Anywhere your information comes from: a person, book, website, advert or video.
The things a source is good at, or does well.
The person or group who made a source; also called the creator.
When a source leans unfairly to one side, often because the maker gains.
Real knowledge of a topic, which makes a source more trustworthy.
How closely a source is really about your issue.
Deciding how useful and trustworthy a source is for a purpose.
A line of choices, such as from strongly agree to strongly disagree.

mistakes: Calling a source simply 'good' or 'bad' instead of asking 'useful for what?'.
Trusting a source just because it looks bright, or comes first in a list.
Forgetting to check who made a source, and why.
Believing an advert as if it were a fair source of facts.
Naming only strengths, or only limitations, instead of both.
Mixing up a fact with an opinion.
Agreeing or disagreeing without giving a reason.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'evaluation' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Evaluation means deciding how useful a source is for a purpose, and how far you can trust it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: The two big questions you ask about every source are 'who?' and '______?'.
questions.modelAnswer: Why? (You ask 'who made it?' and 'why did they make it?'.)

questions.prompt: The reason a source was made is called its ______.
The things a source is good at are its strengths. The things it is not good at are its ______.
True or false: a source is either useful or useless, no matter what your goal is.
questions.modelAnswer: False. A source is useful, or not, for a particular goal; it can be great for one job and poor for another.

questions.prompt: The person or group who made a source is called the ______.
The point of view a source has is called its ______.
Is this a fact or an opinion? 'A can of Mango Fizz has about nine spoons of sugar.'
questions.modelAnswer: A fact. It can be checked on the label.

questions.prompt: Is this a fact or an opinion? 'Homemade smoothies taste much nicer than fizzy drinks.'
questions.modelAnswer: An opinion. Someone could reasonably disagree, because it is about taste.

questions.prompt: To persuade people well, you usually need both facts and ______.
questions.modelAnswer: Opinions (facts and opinions together are the most persuasive).
